## Abstract

Reliable data regarding the association of diabetes mellitus (DM) after heart transplantation (HTx) and infections are lacking. We aimed to assess the association between pre- and post-HTx DM and hospitalizations for infections, mortality, and other secondary outcomes.

Adult HTx recipients from the US Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients transplanted between 1995 and 2021 without previous or multi-organ transplants were included. Uni- and multivariable Cox proportional hazard models were used to assess the association of pre-transplant DM (at HTx) and posttransplant DM compared to no DM with the rate of hospitalizations for infections and all-cause mortality and other secondary outcomes.

A total of 53,219 patients were included, of whom 12,708 (23.9%) had DM at transplantation. Compared to non-diabetic participants, participants with pre-transplant DM were older, more likely to be male and less likely to be of white race. Both, pre- and post-transplant DM was associated with higher rates of hospitalization for infections (hazard ratio [95% confidence interval]: pre-HTx DM: 1.22 [1.18-1.27], post- HTx DM: 1.24 [1.16-1.32] and mortality (1.21 [1.17-1.25] and 1.3 [1.25-1.35], respectively). Both were also associated with higher rates of fatal infections and graft failure.

Pre- and post-transplant DM are associated with higher rates of hospitalizations for infection and mortality after HTx.

## Background

Diabetes Mellitus (DM) is increasingly prevalent globally [1]. Its prevalence and incidence among heart transplant (HTx) recipients are particularly high, with about 20% affected at transplantation and another 20% developing DM after HTx. This disproportionally high prevalence has several reasons, including (i) increased neurohumoral activation in heart failure, leading to higher rates of DM, (ii) immobility due to heart failure raising the risk of DM, and (iii) the required post-HTx immunosuppressive therapies including corticosteroids that increase the likelihood of developing insulin resistance and DM [2–4]. Furthermore, these immunosuppressants make HTx recipients particularly vulnerable to infections [5–7].

Infections are among the major drivers of mortality after HTx, along with graft failure and neoplasms [5]. In the general population, DM is associated with higher rates of infections requiring hospitalization and therapy [8], but in HTx recipients, this association remains unclear as only small, mostly single-center studies have evaluated it and yielded mixed results [7]. Moreover, the potentially different associations between pre- and post-transplant DM and the rate of infections after HTx remain unknown.

Finally, previous analyses assessing the impact of post-transplant DM on other outcomes such as allcause mortality have yielded mixed results and have insufficiently accounted for survivorship bias [2, 7, 9]. Therefore, we examined these associations in a nationally representative sample of US heart

Page 3/17

transplant recipients. We hypothesized that both pre- and post-transplant DM is associated with a higher rate of hospitalizations for infections, all-cause mortality, and other secondary outcomes after HTx.

## Methods

## Study design and study population

This study used data from the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients (SRTR). The SRTR data system includes data on all donor, wait-listed candidates, and transplant recipients in the US, submitted by the members of the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN). The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services provides oversight to the activities of the OPTN and SRTR contractors. All methods in this study were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations.

We included all patients in the SRTR undergoing orthotopic heart transplantation between 1995 and 2021 who (i) were at least 18 years old at transplantation, (ii) had no previous transplants of any organ, and (iii) underwent only heart transplantation and no multi-organ transplants. For the analysis of posttransplant DM, we included a subpopulation of this cohort that had (i) no diabetes at HTx, and (ii) had more than 365 days of follow-up in the SRTR, in line with previous reports [2].

## Pre- and post-transplant DM

The primary exposures were pre- and post-transplant DM. Pre-transplant DM was defined as any documented diagnosis in the waitlist records or records from the hospitalization for the transplant. Patients with unknown diabetes status at transplantation were considered to have no DM (1.8% of the final dataset).

Post-transplant DM was recorded in the annual follow-up record, in which DM status is a prespecified item. The follow-up records note if there has been a new DM diagnosis since the prior visit, and no date of DM diagnosis is provided. Therefore, we used the date of the follow-up visit in which a new DM diagnosis was recorded as the date of DM diagnosis.

## Infections, mortality, and other outcomes

The primary outcomes of interest were (i) the time to hospitalization for infection and (ii) the time to allcause mortality.

In the annual registry follow-up records, providers were asked to report any new health diagnoses, including hospitalization for infections. The date of hospitalization for an infection was coded as the median time point between the last follow-up record without a hospitalization for an infection and the


<!-- Page 4 -->


Page 4/17

first follow-up record with a hospitalization for infection. All-cause mortality and date of death are assessed centrally in the SRTR registry using linkage to the death records.

Secondary outcomes were fatal infections, graft failure, renal replacement therapy, need for dialysis, MACE (defined as fatal or non-fatal stroke or heart disease), stroke, the occurrence of any malignancies, and episodes of acute rejection. These outcomes are recorded in the SRTR annual follow-up records. The follow-up records do not include dates for these events. Similar to DM diagnoses, we classified the date of onset as the date of the follow-up visit with the first record of the outcome of interest.

## Statistical Analyses

First, we examined the association of pre-transplant DM at transplantation with primary and secondary outcomes. Pre-transplant characteristics of patients with and without DM at transplantation were assessed and compared. Pre-transplant DM was included in univariate and multivariable Cox regression models for each respective outcome as a binary exposure variable. Multivariable regression models included the following covariates, chosen a priori: age, gender, race, BMI of the recipient at transplantation; donor age, gender, and race; and the primary diagnosis for HTx (i. e. type of cardiomyopathy, categorized into ischemic, dilated, hypertrophic, congenital, restrictive, valvular, and other cardiomyopathy), and year of transplantation since 1995, included in the models with a natural spline with three degrees of freedom.

Second, to assess the association of post-transplant DM with outcomes and to avoid survivorship bias, post-transplant DM was assessed as a time-varying exposure by splitting the person-time of patients with a post-transplant DM diagnosis and classifying it as unexposed time before their DM diagnosis and exposed time after the diagnosis. Again, we compared the association between DM and outcomes using univariate and multivariable Cox regression using the same covariates.

We conducted several sensitivity analyses, such as stratifying by the median of year of transplantation (2008) and excluding patients with unknown diabetes status at transplantation. To rule out competing risks as the explanation for the inverse association between DM at time of transplantation and the occurrence of malignancies, we used a Fine & Gray subdistribution hazard model. Finally, we assessed whether hazards associated with pre- or post-transplant DM for different outcomes changed during follow-up by constructing multivariable regression models including an interaction term with the logarithm of time since transplant.

All statistical analyses were carried out in RStudio (v2023.06.2, Posit Software, Boston, MA, USA) using R Statistical Software (v4.3.0, R Core Team, 2023) and publicly available software packages. No imputation of missing values was necessary since the percentage of missingness for covariates in multivariable models was low. An alpha level of 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

## Results


<!-- Page 5 -->


Page 5/17

## Study population

Among 79,055 patients in SRTR receiving an orthotopic HTx between 1987 and 2021, 53,219 patients were included in the final analysis (Figure 1). Out of these, 12,708 (23.9%) had DM at HTx. The characteristics of patients with and without DM at transplantation are displayed in Table 1. Characteristics of patients without DM at transplantation, stratified by the development of posttransplant DM are displayed in Supplemental Table 1. Patients who developed post-transplant DM had higher body mass index, had a higher proportion of ischemic cardiomyopathy as the primary diagnosis for HTx, and a lower proportion of higher education than those who did not develop post-transplant DM during follow-up.

## Outcomes According to Diabetes Mellitus Status at Transplantation

Patients with DM at transplantation had higher rates of hospitalizations for infections and all-cause mortality in univariable models compared to patients without DM at transplantation (Figure 2, Table 2).

DM at transplantation was also associated with higher rates of other secondary outcomes in univariate and multivariable models (Table 2). Patients with DM had higher rates of fatal infections, need for dialysis and renal replacement therapies, acute rejection episodes, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) including stroke. They also displayed higher rates of malignancies in a univariate model, but patients with pre-transplant DM had slightly lower rates of malignancies in multivariable models (Table 2) This inverse association remained in the Fine & Gray subdistribution hazard model to account for competing risks (hazard ratio [95% confidence interval]: 0.85 [0.81; 0.89]). The rates of different outcomes for patients with pre-transplant DM were largely unaltered when follow-up was limited to 5 years after HTx in sensitivity analyses (Supplemental Table 3 and 4).

The analysis of the interaction with time indicated increasing association over time between  pretransplant DM and hospitalizations for infections, mortality, fatal infections, dialysis, renal replacement therapy, and stroke (Figure 3).

## Incidence and Outcomes in Post-Transplant Diabetes Mellitus

To examine health risks following post-transplant DM, we included 33,071 patients from the original sample with more than 365 days of follow-up (Figure 1). Out of these, 7491 (22.7%) developed posttransplant DM during the follow-up period. The median time to DM diagnosis was 5.01 years after HTx (interquartile range: 2.03 – 10 years).

The results of univariate and multivariable Cox regression models for post-transplant DM are displayed in Table 3. Post-transplant DM was associated with higher rates of hospitalizations for infections and allcause mortality in both univariate and multivariable models. These associations were slightly stronger than associations for pre-transplant DM. Post-transplant DM was also associated with higher rates of


<!-- Page 6 -->


Page 6/17

fatal infections, graft failure, renal replacement therapy, and dialysis. Post-transplant DM was not associated with higher rates of malignancies, MACE, and stroke. The associations between posttransplant DM and health outcomes increased with a longer duration of follow-up after DM diagnosis for hospitalization for infection, graft failure, dialysis, MACE and stroke (Figure 4). The rates of different outcomes for patients with post-transplant DM were largely unaltered when follow-up was limited to 3 or 5 years after HTx in sensitivity analyses (Supplemental Table 5 and 6).

Contrary to pre-transplant DM, post-transplant DM was associated with lower rates of acute rejection, but the analysis of the interaction with time indicated that this inverse association in post-HTx DM is primarily driven by the first 5 years of follow-up after post-HTx DM diagnosis, after which post-HTx DM is associated with higher rates of acute rejection (Figure 4).

The findings remained unchanged in a sensitivity analysis if only patients with known DM status at transplantation were included (Supplemental Table 7).

## Consistency of Outcomes in Different Transplant Periods

To differentiate whether the year of transplantation including associated post-transplant treatment regimens and management may impact the association between pre- and post-transplant diabetes mellitus, we analyzed the hazard ratios for all outcomes of interest in 4-year periods starting 1995 (Supplemental Figure S2 and S3). Interestingly, the rates of dialysis, MACE, and stroke associated with both, pre- and post-transplant DM decayed in later transplant periods, while the association between diabetes, infections and mortality remained consistent over different years of transplantation.

We also assessed the effect sizes according to different transplant periods by splitting the whole study population according to its median year of transplantation. Thus, the population was split into patients transplanted before 2009 and 2009 and after. The associations with infections and mortality seen across both periods remained stable for both, pre- and port-transplant DM with only minor deviations in effect sizes even though the person-time of follow-up was lower in the 2009-2021 period (Supplemental Table 8 and 9). However, again, the rates of stroke, dialysis and MACE associated with diabetes were lower in the 2009-2021 period (Supplemental Table 5 and 6).

Finally, when we assessed whether the year of transplant itself was related to various outcomes in the multivariable regression models (Supplemental Figure S4 and S5), the estimates were highly alike in both, the pre- and post-transplantation diabetes mellitus models. Specifically, the risk of infection, death and fatal infection tended to decrease slightly in later transplant periods but no major association of the year of transplant with these outcomes was detected. There was also no relevant association of the year of transplantation with graft failure, malignancies, dialysis and MACE, even though there was a tendency for increasing risk in later transplant years. Stroke risk decreased until 2010 but this decrease stopped afterwards. The rate of confirmed acute rejection episodes was lower in patients transplanted earlier as opposed to patients transplanted more recently.

## Discussion

In this study, we examined contemporary data on the associations of pre- and post-transplant DM with hospitalizations for infections, all-cause mortality, and other secondary outcomes after HTx among transplant recipients in the United States. Both pre- and post-transplant DM are associated with higher rates of infections and all-cause mortality after HTx. For secondary outcomes, both pre- and posttransplant DM are associated with higher rates of fatal infection, and the need for renal replacement therapy but not with higher rates of neoplasms. While pre-transplant DM is associated with higher rates of MACE, stroke and acute rejection episodes, these associations were not seen in post-transplant DM, potentially due to shorter follow-up duration after post-HTx DM diagnosis.

## Incidence of Post-Transplant Diabetes Mellitus

Out of all patients without DM at time of heart transplantation included in this analysis, who survived the first year after transplantation, every fourth patient developed post-transplant DM. These numbers are broadly consistent with previous reports and are a display of the high risk of developing DM in this population [2, 10, 11]. This elevated risk is largely attributable to side effects of immunosuppressive therapies used in this setting, which is also applicable to populations transplanted with other solid organs [12]. Particularly, prolonged use of corticoids and the use of tacrolimus over ciclosporin may be linked to higher risk of post-transplant DM [2], whereas there is no clear evidence for a higher risk of post-transplant DM in patients undergoing induction immunosuppression [13]. In addition, typical comorbidities such as ischemic heart disease, obesity, as well as demographic risk factors such as male sex and higher age are associated with the development of DM post heart transplantation [2]. Yet, this analysis focused more on the implications of pre- and post-transplant DM rather than on the risk factors which have been analyzed in multiple previous reports [2, 10–12, 14, 15]. Diabetes Mellitus and Infections after HTx

We found a consistent association between pre- and post-transplant DM and hospitalizations for infections after HTx. In sensitivity analyses, these associations persisted in different transplant periods and in adjusted multivariable models. When accounting for potential interaction with the time after transplantation, the association was apparent shortly after Htx in patients with pre-transplant DM and after diagnosis of post-transplant DM and remained stable onwards. The associations were comparable between pre- and post-transplant DM. However, the rate of fatal infections was higher in post-transplant DM patients compared to non-DM than in pre-transplant DM patients compared to non-DM in multivariable regression models.

Although others have investigated the association between post-transplant DM and infections after Htx, the data were inconclusive. Previous reports examined small, mostly single-center cohorts with shorter lengths of follow-up [7]. For example, three studies each included fewer than 400 recipients, and they did not observe statistically significant associations between post-transplant DM and infections, even though trends in that direction were detected [16–18]. A study of 194 HTx recipients reported that post-


<!-- Page 8 -->


Page 8/17

transplant DM was associated with an about two-fold higher rate of infections over a mean follow-up of 64 months [19]. Finally, in a cohort of 391 patients, rate of cardiomegaly virus (CMV)-associated infections were 38% higher in HTx recipients with post-transplant DM [10]. Post-transplant Diabetes Mellitus and Mortality after HTx

We found that compared to no DM, post-transplant DM was associated with higher mortality rates after HTx. The magnitude of this association was slightly greater than in patients with pre-transplant DM. The association between pre-transplant DM and all-cause mortality increased over time, whereas the association between post-HTx DM and mortality remained constant after diagnosis. These findings are in line with recent reports indicating higher mortality rates in HTx recipients with post-transplant DM [2, 10, 18], unlike older analyses in small cohorts which did not find statistically significant associations, potentially due to limited power and follow-up [9, 17, 19]. The largest study on this topic included 26,263 patients from the thoracic transplant registry (TTX) of the International Society of Heart & Lung Transplantation (ISHLT) who received transplants between 1995 and 2017, of whom 5,422 developed post-transplant DM during follow-up [2]. Associations were similar in that study to our findings in the SRTR, but the methodology differed in that in the present report we analyzed DM as a time-varying exposure variable to minimize concerns of survivorship bias [10]. Pre- and post-transplant Diabetes Mellitus and secondary outcomes after HTx

The association between pre- and post-transplant DM and renal outcomes has been previously described [2, 7]. However, the excess risk of requiring dialysis associated with both, pre- and posttransplant DM clearly decreased in later transplant periods. Potential factors that could explain these improvements comprise more individualized management strategies for patients with diabetic kidney disease and novel immunosuppressants with targeted dosing regimens. Novel antihyperglycemic agents such as glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists or sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors with cardiovascular and renal protective effects [20–22] have been introduced in the latest period observed in this study (2015–2020) and may have in part contributed to the lower diabetes-associated risk for these cardiovascular and renal outcomes. However, the diabetes-associated risk for these outcomes already showed a tendency of decrease in the periods before so the introduction of these agents likely does not suffice to explain the risk reduction seen in more recent transplant periods.

Our data do not hint towards an association between the rate of malignancies and DM in HTx patients. While pre-transplant DM was associated with higher rates of malignancies in univariate analyses, this was not the case in multivariable models where the rate of malignancies even tended to be lower. While it cannot be precluded that these associations reflect by a biological phenomenon of diabetesassociated protection against malignancies, it is more likely explained by statistical effects (e. g. collinearity with other covariates) and reporting bias.


<!-- Page 9 -->


Page 9/17

While pre-transplant diabetes mellitus was associated with higher rates of acute rejection episodes, post-transplant diabetes was associated with lower rates of this outcome. The latter is likely explained by the fact that acute rejection episodes mostly occur early, i. e. within months, after HTx, whereas posttransplant diabetes may not even be apparent at that stage. Participants who developed post-transplant DM were already at lower risk of acute rejection episodes at that point. Thus, we regard the lower rates of acute rejection episodes in post-transplant DM as attributable to the handling of diabetes as a timevarying exposure. This assumption is supported by our analysis of the associations between rates of acute rejection episodes and post-HTx DM, which indicated strongly varying hazards over time with lower risk within the first years after transplantation and higher risk later on.

While the magnitutide of the associations between pre-transplant DM and MACE and stroke were similar to the associations between post-transplant DM and these outcomes, they were not statistically significant in post-transplant DM across the whole follow-up. These findings may be explained by the limited follow-up of patients with post-transplant DM but also by time-varying hazards, as the hazards for both MACE and stroke increased significantly over time in this population. In addition, the data indicated that the diabetes-associated risk of MACE and stroke tended to decrease in later transplant periods. Strengths and Limitations

Major strengths of this analysis are the large sample size, analysis of post-transplant DM as a timevarying exposure to address survivorship bias, and the assessment of hazards over time. Thus, this is the first study to comprehensively examine associations between pre- and post-transplant DM and infections, mortality, and other secondary outcomes after HTx. However, this report also comes with several limitations. The adjudication of exposure and outcome events was based on retrospective intake forms. Due to the retrospective nature of the data source and the mode of data entry, we were not able to assess other potentially important aspects of interest. These include granularity in terms of exposures such as hemoglobin A1c levels or antihyperglycemic co-medication and no information on the specific

type of infections, severity, and trajectories. Of note, transplant centers may have strict regulations regarding hemoglobin A1c levels for transplant eligibility prior to HTx, but the glycemic control may be

less rigid and routine screening for diabetes may not occur frequently after the transplantation which could potentially affect the here-presented estimates. While we accounted for several covariates in our multivariable models, residual confounding remains a concern. In addition, the SRTR only obtains data from participating sites in the US. Thus, whether these here-reported associations also apply to non-US populations remains subject to future research. Furthermore, changes of therapeutic regimens of immunosuppressants over transplant periods or over the course of the patients after transplantation were not assessible in this analysis. Finally, due to the rise of new antihyperglycemic agents such as glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists or sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors in recent years [7, 20–22], it remains uncertain whether these associations remain stable among recipients receiving these newer medications.

## Conclusion


<!-- Page 10 -->


Page 10/17

In this large multicenter study of US HTx recipients, pre- and post-HTx DM were associated with higher rates of hospitalizations for infections, mortality, fatal infections, and renal replacement therapy. These findings suggest that there is a need for further preventive and therapeutic interventions in this vulnerable population. Future research is required to investigate whether these associations are applicable to non-US populations and among recipients receiving recently introduced antihyperglycemic medications.
